extracted.intended_audience: writers, literary critics, editors, and clergy (preachers)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and evaluative guidance on poetic, dramatic, and sermonic composition and criticism, with ancillary remarks on translation, editing, and professional ethics. Focuses on what constitutes genius, good character-drawing, unity/progression, and proper tone in sermons and literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion of genius: progression and evolution
rubrics_metrics.description: You will find this a good gage or criterion of genius,--whether it progresses and evolves, or only spins upon itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Dryden's Achitophel and Zimri (every line adds/ modifies the character; a-building up to the last verse) vs Pope's Timon (the first two or three couplets contain all the pith and the rest merely prove overt acts). Use ongoing development across a work to judge 'genius' rather than static cleverness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character-building across lines (progressive characterization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every line adds to or modifies the character, which is, as it were, a-building up to the very last verse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preferred pattern: incremental revelation and modification of character across the text. Anti-pattern: characters presented fully-formed at the outset and merely illustrated thereafter (e.g., Pope's Timon). Compare Lamb's criticisms (exquisite, progressive) with Hazlitt's repeated imitations which 'round and round' but do not evolve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic imagery should be worthy of the poet's powers
rubrics_metrics.description: An image which the necessities of the painter justified, but which was wholly unworthy, in my judgment, of the enlarged powers of the poet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid importing painter's contrivances that limit poetic imagination. Good pictorial passages are those that suit the poet's scope (examples given: Adam bending over the sleeping Eve; Dalilah approaching Samson are cited as proper pictures in Milton). Poor example: Milton's copying of the Sistine fresco lion—justified for a painter but unworthy of great poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liturgical/service language should move genuinely
rubrics_metrics.description: I think the baptismal service almost perfect... I never could attend a christening without tears bursting forth at the sight of the helpless innocent in a pious clergyman's arms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for liturgical wording: it may contain harmless assumptions but should be capable of producing sincere emotional response. Emotional power here is a virtue, not an error, provided it is appropriate to the occasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Didactic poetry must be seasoned with personal interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere didactics of practice, unless seasoned with the personal interests of the time or author, are inexpressibly dull to me.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Didactic verse (like Georgics) needs the author's personal engagement or the flavor of its time to avoid dullness; pure practical instruction in verse without personal/temporal interest is likely lifeless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genius aims at the metaphysical/ideal
rubrics_metrics.description: All genius is metaphysical; because the ultimate end of genius is ideal, however it may be actualized by incidental and accidental circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing 'genius', look for orientation toward the ideal or metaphysical ends, not merely technical accomplishment or accidental effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character contrast: imagination and reason vs common sense
rubrics_metrics.description: Don Quixote is... a man in whom the imagination and the pure reason are so powerful as to make him disregard the evidence of sense when it opposed their conclusions. Sancho is the common sense of the social man-animal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use contrasts between intellectual forces (imagination/reason) and practical common sense to construct vivid, philosophically telling characters; Sancho as foil to Quixote exemplifies this technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sermons must distinguish between 'sin' (nature) and 'sins' (acts)
rubrics_metrics.description: One mistake... is to confound sin with sins. To tell a modest girl... that she is full of sins... is monstrous... But to tell her that she, and all men and women, are of a sinful nature... is true and proper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pastoral rhetoric should avoid accusatory language about particular acts when addressing ordinary people; emphasize the doctrine of sinful nature carefully and sensitively to avoid unwarrantable moral shock.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preaching must infuse the indispensableness of a holy life
rubrics_metrics.description: No article of faith can be truly and duly preached without necessarily and simultaneously infusing a deep sense of the indispensableness of a holy life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Doctrinal preaching should always connect belief to ethical transformation and the practical necessities of holy living; faith taught in abstraction is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotion in sermons only as consequence of reason/understanding/will
rubrics_metrics.description: Every attempt, in a sermon, to cause emotion, except as the consequence of an impression made on the reason, or the understanding, or the will, I hold to be fanatical and sectarian.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid manipulative or purely emotive preaching; any emotional effect should arise naturally from reasoned argument and moral appeal rather than being an end in itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extempore preaching is risky unless the preacher can sustain argument
rubrics_metrics.description: No doubt preaching, in the proper sense of the word, is more effective than reading; and, therefore, I would not prohibit it... but I never yet heard more than one preacher without book, who did not forget his argument in three minutes' time; and fall into vague and unprofitable declamation...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow extempore preaching but recognise its dangers: many extempore preachers lack structure and lapse into sterility. If a preacher cannot sustain a clear argument extempore, prefer well-prepared reading or rigorous training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity, causation, and progression in long poems/dramas
rubrics_metrics.description: There is neither causation nor progression in the Faust;... The scenes are mere magic-lantern pictures, and a large part of the work is... very flat. There is no whole in the poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A large-scale poetic or dramatic work should exhibit causal links, logical progression, and an overall unity; avoid assembling merely picturesque or episodic scenes without connective growth or purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protagonist needs credible development (avoid ready-made figures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Faust himself is dull and meaningless... he is a ready-made conjuror from the very beginning; the incredulus odi is felt from the first line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid presenting the central figure as already complete and simply demonstrated; the protagonist should undergo change, have motivating causes, and develop across the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer verse over prose for translating poetry (where language allows)
rubrics_metrics.description: I do not admit the argument for prose translations. I would in general rather see verse attempted in so capable a language as ours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When translating poetic works (e.g., Faust) into a language capable of verse, attempt metrical/verse translation rather than prosy paraphrase to better preserve poetic qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Romantic drama: dialogue and character over artificial plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Beaumont and Fletcher's plots are, to be sure, wholly inartificial; they only care to pitch a character into a position to make him or her talk; you must swallow all their gross improbabilities... attend only to the dialogue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In certain romantic-dramatic modes, accept implausible plotting as a device to enable characterful dialogue; craft dialogue to carry the play's interest even when plot artifice is weak.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shakespeare's universality resists mannered imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Shakspeare... is universal, and, in fact, has no manner; just as you can so much more readily copy a picture than Nature herself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt mechanical imitation of Shakespeare's 'manner'—his universality is not a replicable style. Study his principles (universality, depth) rather than surface effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand dramatic style positions (Massinger — Samson Agonistes spectrum)
rubrics_metrics.description: The styles of Massinger's plays and the Sampson Agonistes are the two extremes of the arc within which the diction of dramatic poetry may oscillate. Shakspeare in his great plays is the midpoint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be conscious of where a work sits on a formal/style spectrum (colloquial vs heightened diction) and choose the appropriate diction for plausibility and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best physicians in nervous cases inspire hope
rubrics_metrics.description: In the treatment of nervous cases, he is the best physician, who is the most ingenious inspirer of hope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Therapeutic value often lies in the physician's ability to instil hope and confidence; bedside manner and encouragement are clinical tools, especially in nervous or psychosomatic cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: High-risk surgery requires extraordinary certainty/ethics
rubrics_metrics.description: I think there are only two things wanting to justify a surgeon in performing the Caesarean operation: first, that he should possess infallible knowledge of his art: and, secondly, that he should be infallibly certain that he is infallible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although hyperbolic, this asserts a strong ethical principle: operations with grave risks demand exceptional assurance of skill and cautious ethical justification; emphasises weighty responsibility in surgical decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial duty: preserve and restore original verse/prose in editions
rubrics_metrics.description: How lamentable it is that no gentleman and scholar can be found to edit these beautiful plays!... There are whole scenes in their edition which I could with certainty put back into their original verse...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should undertake careful scholarly restoration of texts (especially dramatists) rather than careless modernizing or corrupt editions; the editorial task is a duty to literary fidelity.
